beats.intro: Chapter nine, lesson three. The stages of cellular respiration. [[mill]]Think of a water mill on a stream. The water does not turn the wheel in one jump. It passes through a series of stages, and the work is done along the way. [[map]]Cellular respiration is like that. Here is the map from lesson one, with its parts still dim. [[lit]]Today we light it up, stage by stage, and then follow one glucose all the way through.
beats.three: [[say]]Cellular respiration has three stages. [[g]]Glycolysis breaks glucose into two pyruvate. [[c]]The citric acid cycle completes the breakdown of glucose. [[o]]And oxidative phosphorylation accounts for most of the ATP. [[four]]Now look at the map. It shows a fourth box, between glycolysis and the cycle, called pyruvate oxidation. It is a bridge, a short link step, so the slides count three stages, and the map shows the bridge between them. Both are correct.
beats.glyco: [[cyto]]Stage one happens in the cytosol, the fluid outside the mitochondrion. [[glc]]One glucose, a sugar with six carbons, goes in. [[split]]Glycolysis splits it, and two pyruvate come out. [[nadh]]It also loads a little energy onto the carrier N A D H, which we met in lesson two. [[atp1]]And it makes a small amount of ATP right there, which we will come back to.
beats.mito: [[enter]]If oxygen is present, the pyruvate moves into the mitochondrion. [[ox]]There, pyruvate oxidation turns each pyruvate into acetyl co-A. The slide does not draw it, but this step also loads a carrier, so it makes N A D H too. [[cycle]]Acetyl co-A feeds the citric acid cycle, a wheel in the matrix, the inner space of the mitochondrion. The cycle completes the breakdown of glucose, and the carriers it fills are N A D H and F A D H 2. [[ox2]]The last stage, oxidative phosphorylation, sits in the inner membrane. Its two parts are electron transport and chemiosmosis, and lessons six and seven take them apart.
beats.carriers: [[ac]]Now follow the white paths on the map. [[nad1]]Glycolysis sends its electrons by N A D H. [[nad2]]The citric acid cycle sends its electrons by N A D H and F A D H 2. [[over]]All of them run to the last stage. Think of the carriers as shuttle buses, and the inner membrane as the terminal where they unload. That is why oxidative phosphorylation is the powerhouse. It is where the electrons fall in energy, and the fall is used to make ATP.
beats.q1: Quick check. Where does glycolysis take place?
beats.atp: [[stars]]Now the ATP. The map has three stars at the bottom, one under each of three stages. [[s1]]Under glycolysis, a small amount of ATP. [[s2]]Under the citric acid cycle, another small amount. [[s3]]Under oxidative phosphorylation, a very large burst. [[ninety]]It accounts for almost ninety percent of the ATP made by cellular respiration. So do not judge a stage by how famous it is. Judge it by how much ATP it makes.
beats.compare: [[two]]The map names two ways to make ATP. [[sub]]The first is substrate-level phosphorylation. An enzyme holds a substrate that carries a phosphate group. The enzyme moves that phosphate straight to A D P. Out comes ATP, and a product. One enzyme, one hand-off, no carriers needed. [[subwhere]]It happens in glycolysis and in the citric acid cycle, and it gives the smaller amount. [[ox3]]The second is oxidative phosphorylation. Here no enzyme passes a phosphate across. Instead, the ATP is powered by redox reactions, the electron transfers we saw in lesson one, and that is how it gets its name. [[table]]So, substrate-level is a direct hand-off, small, and in two stages. Oxidative is powered by redox, large, and in the last stage.
beats.q2: Quick check. Which stage makes most of the ATP?
beats.walk: [[start]]Let us follow one glucose through the whole map. [[w1]]It starts in the cytosol with six carbons. Glycolysis splits it into two pyruvate, three carbons each. A little ATP is made, and two carriers are filled with electrons. [[w2]]The pyruvate enters the mitochondrion. Each loses a carbon as carbon dioxide and becomes acetyl co-A, with another carrier filled. [[w3]]The acetyl groups go round the citric acid cycle. More carbon dioxide leaves, a little more ATP is made, and many more carriers are filled.
beats.walk2: [[w4]]By now all six carbons of the glucose have left as carbon dioxide. But most of the energy has not been spent. It rides on the carriers. [[w5]]They unload at the inner membrane, the electrons fall, and oxidative phosphorylation makes the large burst of ATP.
beats.walk3: [[w6]]Textbooks put the total at about thirty ATP per glucose. That figure is from the textbook, not these slides, and lesson seven will count it properly.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[s1]]Respiration has three stages: glycolysis in the cytosol, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation, with pyruvate oxidation as the bridge. [[s2]]The carriers N A D H and F A D H 2 bring electrons to the last stage, which makes almost ninety percent of the ATP. [[s3]]Substrate-level phosphorylation is a direct phosphate hand-off. Oxidative phosphorylation is powered by redox. [[end]]Now try the practice.
